summary.note: Ten merged pull requests (#459-#482) re-read diff by diff against Go tailscaled and the tailscale CLI at the release this repository's own parity ledger pins, v1.102.4, cloned shallow at that commit. Four are faithful. Six diverge from the upstream behaviour their own diff claims to port, and seven findings record the Go path and the ref each was read at. Three of the seven are disclosed in the commit body that carries them; they are recorded anyway, because a divergence a reader has to find in a paragraph of prose is not tracked work.

auditedPrs.notes: Ports Go startLocked's third auth-key source. The guards match clause for clause: the key is trimmed, a Running node and a --config-driven node are refused, and an already-enrolled node is refused unless control is asking it to log in again (Go's len(Profiles()) == 0 || state == NeedsLogin, inverted into the refusal). Policy is consulted last, behind the explicit flag, TS_AUTH_KEY and the config file, which is Go's order. The one deliberate divergence -- a whitespace-only key reads as not configured, where Go passes its non-empty test and then assigns the trimmed empty string -- leaves the same empty auth key on both sides and differs only in which log line is written, so it is not filed.

Data and test only: it replaces PARITY_AUDIT.json's contents and generalises tests/parity_audit_ledger.rs so the ledger contract no longer pins one edition's pull request number. It claims no Go port, so there is no upstream behaviour to diverge from. The contract it leaves behind is real and this edition satisfies it: stated totals recomputed from the rows, a verdict backed by the presence or absence of findings, every named divergence written up, and every upstream citation anchored to one 40-character commit.

The headline port is right: the empty-address check now runs before the -1 truncation and before the family filter, as Go's runIP does, it carries Go's 'no current Tailscale IPs; state: %v' text, and the peer, Service and self paths all reach it. Two of runIP's other error returns did not come with it. The mutually exclusive flag refusal still leaves through main's Result and so still wears the Error: prefix the commit body names as the defect it removed, and the --assert arm keeps a message and a comparison that are neither Go's.

The nil-versus-empty port is faithful: advertise_routes is an Option, an explicit [] replaces the pref and withdraws every route, and an absent key or an explicit null leaves it alone, which is exactly what Go's guard and Go's JSON decoding do. The refusal is wrapped once in Go's caller-side wording and names the parsed prefix, both correct. What did not move is the other half of the same guard: with an absent AdvertiseRoutes key the validation still judges the routes already in prefs, which upstream never looks at. The commit body records that as deliberate and out of scope.

The missing step is genuinely restored and in Go's shape: the prefs read, the --readonly and already-on skips, a failed read counting as off, Go's wrapped 'starting web client in tailscaled: ' error, the address rendered as an AddrPort with 'invalid AddrPort' for a node with none, and the interrupt-time reset confined to a listener run that turned the pref on. Adding --readonly to the CGI test helper is the right correction. What differs is the shape of the two lines on the wire: Go writes them through the standard log package with its default log prefix, and this build writes them bare.

The framing is exact -- the cause under Go's 'error: ' prefix, Go's blank line, then the help pointer, written once by the new entry point and exiting 1 rather than propagating as a single Error: line -- and moving this build's --service refusal behind Go's own checks, and cleaning the mount point before the listener is resolved, both put the right refusal first. The sequence is still not serve_v2.go's, because one of its steps does not exist here: verifyFunnelEnabled runs between the two --service refusals upstream and has no counterpart anywhere in this build.

All three message defects are really fixed and the ports behind them hold up. go_io_error_text drops Rust's os-error suffix and lower-cases the first character, which is the whole difference between Rust's strerror rendering and Go's errno table for the errnos this path can produce. go_mkdir_all reproduces os.MkdirAll for its error rather than its effect, and matches it step for step: the Stat fast path, ENOTDIR named against the component in the way, the string-wise parent walk with the same termination condition, and the Lstat re-check that treats a level lost to a concurrent creator as created. Omitting Go's sandboxed-macOS arm is legitimate -- there is no sandboxed GUI build here to reach it.

The verification is accurate as far as it goes. The decoded list is read rather than the rendered report row, the nil-versus-empty rule is right in both directions, and an undecodable list becoming no restriction really is what Go's error path produces, since the caller of fillAllowedSuggestions keeps the nil and only logs. But the pull request's own subject -- that exit-node suggest already honours the allow-list -- is broader than what is there: upstream honours it by filtering candidates before it ranks them, and this build honours it by withholding the engine's single answer afterwards. The allow-list candidate filter is the half that is missing, and the commit body files it as an engine ask rather than claiming it.

Documentation plus a guard-test entry; no behaviour changed, and the behaviour it describes is the one in the tree. The precedence it writes down -- policy AuthKey consulted last, behind an explicit key, the environment and the config file -- is Go's order in startLocked, and calling that an inversion of how policy ranks for prefs is correct rather than an excuse. Adding AuthKey to the definition-type guard and exercising a load over a state directory with no profile in it both pin preconditions the auth-key path depends on and nothing else covered.

The completion is confirmed correctly and the confirmation is worth having: the condition really is a colon test rather than a tag: prefix test, so a value like foo:bar reaches the validator and is refused by name instead of becoming a tag nobody asked for, and both daemon entry points write the completed list back before anything is persisted. The four validation clauses match upstream one for one. The CheckTag wording does not: every refusal here is re-worded, so none of the four sentences a Go-facing script or runbook matches on is produced.

gate.detail: Run on main at b41721d with the pinned stable toolchain 1.95.0 (clippy is not installed for the nightly default on this machine). cargo fmt --all --check clean; cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings clean; cargo test --all-targets 37 binaries all `test result: ok`, including the 618-test lib binary and the six parity_audit_ledger tests over this file; cargo build --release --bins finished in 7m 43s. One caveat, environmental and not a fault on main: with the session's own deep TMPDIR, tailnetd's cleanup_refuses_live_socket aborts the test step with `path must be shorter than SUN_LEN` -- it builds a Unix socket path under std::env::temp_dir() that came to 109 bytes against the 104-byte limit. Re-run with a short TMPDIR it passes with everything else.

findings.title: verifyFunnelEnabled is absent from the ported check sequence
findings.detail: runServeCombined runs, in order: the --service-with-funnel refusal, verifyFunnelEnabled(ctx, 443) when the subcommand is funnel, the --service-without-background refusal, cleanURLPath, then srvTypeAndPortFromFlags. The merged check_serve_flags -- whose own doc comment claims to run serve_v2.go's checks in serve_v2.go's order -- places the two --service refusals adjacent and has no funnel-eligibility step at all. CheckFunnelAccess, NodeCanFunnel and CheckFunnelPort have no counterpart anywhere in this build, so tnet funnel on a node lacking CapabilityHTTPS or NodeAttrFunnel never produces 'Funnel not available; HTTPS must be enabled.' or 'port N is not allowed for funnel', and a command line such as tnet funnel --tcp=70000 3000 reaches the usage framing this change added where Go refuses earlier, with the funnel error.

findings.title: The policy allow-list withholds a suggestion instead of filtering candidates
findings.detail: Upstream applies the list inside the ranking: suggestExitNodeUsingDERP hands AppendMatchingPeers a predicate that drops any peer for which allowList is non-nil and does not contain its StableID, so what comes back is the best node the administrator permits. This build asks the engine for one suggestion and then withholds it in diag::permitted_suggestion when the list excludes it. On a tailnet whose top-ranked exit node is excluded, upstream suggests the next permitted node and this build suggests nothing -- which reads to the operator as 'no exit node available' rather than as a policy decision. The commit body discloses this and files the missing half as an engine ask, so it is not a claim the pull request makes falsely; the allow-list candidate filter is still absent, which is what the row records.

findings.title: The mutually exclusive flag refusal still prints with an Error: prefix
findings.detail: runIP returns 'tailscale ip -1, -4, and -6 are mutually exclusive' and the CLI's main prints a returned error with a bare fmt.Fprintln to stderr before exiting 1, so Go's text carries no prefix. The merged change routed only the new IpUnanswered errors through eprintln! plus a direct exit; ip_usage_refusal still uses anyhow::bail!, so that refusal travels out through main's Result and stderr reads 'Error: tnet ip -1, -4, and -6 are mutually exclusive'. That Error: prefix on a runIP return is exactly the defect the commit body states this change removes, left standing on the one refusal in the same function that the change did not touch.

findings.title: The --assert arm keeps neither Go's wording nor Go's comparison
findings.detail: runIP's --assert arm compares ip.String() against the flag value over the node's own st.TailscaleIPs and, on a miss, returns 'assertion failed: IP %q not found among %v', which main prints bare. The merged run_ip prints 'assertion failed: this node does not hold <ip>' -- neither Go's wording nor the list of addresses Go shows the reader -- and compares parsed IpAddr values, so a non-canonical spelling such as 100.064.000.001 asserts successfully where Go's exact string comparison refuses it. tnet also makes --assert conflict with a peer argument at parse time, where Go accepts both and silently ignores the peer, since the assert arm returns before the peer is resolved.

findings.title: An absent AdvertiseRoutes key still validates the routes already in prefs
findings.detail: ToPrefs runs the masking check only over c.AdvertiseRoutes, inside the nil guard this change ports; nothing in it reads the prefs the config is layered onto, so a Go config that says nothing about routes cannot be refused over a route already on disk. The merged Config::apply_to_prefs ports the guard for the write but keeps the pre-existing fallback for the validation: with an absent AdvertiseRoutes key it judges prefs.advertise_routes, so a node holding a lone default route in one family fails to boot on a config that never mentions routes -- a refusal upstream has no way to produce. The commit body records this as deliberate and out of scope, which makes it a known divergence rather than an oversight, but it is still one inside the block this change re-shaped.

findings.title: The web-client start and stop lines are missing Go's log prefix
findings.detail: runWeb emits both 'starting tailscaled web client at http://...' and 'stopping tailscaled web client' through the standard log package. Nothing on the tailscale web path resets that logger: the only log.SetFlags(0) in cmd/tailscale/cli/cli.go sits inside fatalf, and the two others are in file.go and cert.go, neither of which runWeb reaches. So Go's stderr carries the default date-and-time log prefix on both lines. The merged start_tailscaled_web_client writes them bare with eprintln!, and the new tests assert the bare form as the Go-parity outcome, which pins a shape Go does not produce.

findings.title: The tag refusals do not carry Go's CheckTag wording
findings.detail: prefsFromUpArgs wraps every tag failure as 'tag: %q: %s' around one of CheckTag's four messages: tags must start with 'tag:', tag names must not be empty, tag names must start with a letter after 'tag:', and tag names can only contain numbers, letters, or dashes. complete_and_validate_advertise_tags reproduces the completion and all four clauses faithfully but emits 'invalid tag "x": ...' with four re-worded reasons, so none of the four sentences Go produces is produced here. The commit body describes the message shape as aligned with upstream's tag: %q; what is aligned is the quoting of the completed value, not the CheckTag wording behind it, and a runbook or script written against the Go CLI matches on the latter.
